name: Treaty with the Tribes of Middle Oregon, 1855 (Warm Springs Treaty)
aka: Treaty with the Confederated Tribes of Middle Oregon
nations: Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon (Warm Springs and Wasco bands)
promises: Article 1 set apart the Warm Springs reservation for the bands' exclusive use, closed to white residents without the agent's and superintendent's permission.

Article 1 secured the exclusive right of taking fish in streams through and bordering the reservation and at all other usual and accustomed stations in common with citizens, with hunting, gathering and pasturing on unclaimed lands.
Article 2: annual payments over twenty years, from $8,000 a year falling to $2,000.
Article 4: a sawmill and flouring mill, hospital, school, shops, and their staff for twenty years.

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission found that the 1,605,000 acres of the award area ceded by this treaty were worth $1,650,000 when the treaty took effect on March 8, 1859, and that the $313,682.70 the United States paid was an unconscionable consideration.

landTaken: The Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs state about ten million acres were relinquished (CTWS, History). The Indian Claims Commission's award area was 1,605,000 acres along the south shore of the Columbia (Docket 198, 1972).
compensation: $1,225,000 final award (ICC Docket 198, 1973), by stipulated settlement after the 1972 finding of unconscionable consideration.

nationVoice.nation: Confederated Tribes of the Warm Springs Reservation of Oregon
nationVoice.summary: The Tribes say the 1855 treaty came from orders to clear Indians from their land, and that they reserved the reservation for exclusive use and kept their rights at usual and accustomed places.

plain.promised: The Warm Springs reservation for the bands' exclusive use, the right of taking fish at usual and accustomed stations, yearly payments over twenty years, and mills, a hospital and a school.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1972 that the 1,605,000 acres it considered were worth $1,650,000 and that the $313,682.70 the United States paid was unconscionable.
plain.today: A final award of $1,225,000 was entered in 1973 by settlement. What has happened since has not been researched.

openQuestions: The 1865 supplementary treaty (Huntington treaty), by which the bands were recorded as giving up off-reservation fishing and travel rights, was not researched; Docket 198-A was dismissed in 1970 and its subject was not read.
The flooding of Celilo Falls and other Columbia fishing sites by dams, and Columbia River fishing cases (Sohappy v. Smith / United States v. Oregon), were not researched in this pass.

Audit 2026-11-08: the 1973 final award changed from claims-commission to litigation, because the Commission entered it on a stipulated settlement (Docket 198, Final Award, October 17, 1973). The 1972 finding of unconscionable consideration stands as the claims-commission finding.
